opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame recursive self-improvement, the idea of AI systems doing AI research to improve themselves, as two questions: whether it's possible in principle, and what's actually happening in practice.

In principle, I think it's a reasonable direction. A lot of AI research today is quite mechanical. You propose a small architectural change, run a sweep, read the loss curves, and iterate. Much of that loop can be automated, and we're already seeing systems that write experiment code, tune hyperparameters, and draft papers. So I don't think it's science fiction that parts of the research pipeline will close into a loop.

But I'm more cautious than some people on two points.

First, there's a difference between *search* and *understanding*. Current automated research mostly scales up search. It tries many things and keeps what works on some benchmark. That can produce real gains, but it tends to stay inside the space we already defined: the same metrics, the same kinds of models. The big jumps in science usually come from someone noticing that the question itself is wrong, or finding a new representation that makes things simple. My own interest in interpretability and in what I'd call "physics of AI" comes from this. I care whether we understand why something works, not only that it works. I haven't yet seen a convincing case where an automated system produced that kind of conceptual reframing.

Second, there's the evaluation bottleneck. A self-improving loop is only as good as its feedback signal. If the signal is a benchmark, the system will overfit to the benchmark, which is Goodhart's law. If the signal is "does this generalize to genuinely new problems," that is expensive and slow to measure, and it's hard to automate. So I suspect the speed of recursive improvement will be limited less by how smart the agent is and more by how fast and how honestly we can evaluate progress.

So my overall view is that it's promising as an accelerator. It will make good researchers much more productive and handle a lot of the engineering grind. I'm skeptical of the strong version, where it takes off on its own. For the field, I think the most valuable work is building better ways to verify and understand what these systems discover. Otherwise we may get a lot of improvement that we can't trust and can't explain. And that also matters a great deal for safety.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts search with understanding generally, but does not state that remembering failed experiments fails to show why they failed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think RSI, recursive self-improvement, is one of those ideas that sounds very clean on a whiteboard and gets much messier the moment you actually try to build it. The vision is simple: you have an AI that does AI research, it finds a better training recipe or a better architecture, you train the next model with it, and that model is a better researcher, and so on. The loop closes and things accelerate.

My honest assessment is that the loop is real, but it's much more partial and much more bottlenecked than people assume.

First, what has actually worked. If you look at what "automated AI research" means today, most of the wins are in the parts of research that are closest to search. Hyperparameter sweeps, architecture search within a fixed space, writing and debugging experiment code, scanning the literature, proposing variations on an existing idea. Models are already quite good at that, and it genuinely compounds. A lab that uses models to write their infra and run ten times more ablations per week is doing faster science. That's a meaningful speedup, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But I would separate "doing a lot of experiments" from "knowing which experiment matters." The hard part of research, at least the research I care about, is choosing the question and building the right abstraction. When I worked on things like KANs or on trying to understand grokking, the bottleneck was never generating candidates. It was having a mental model of why something should work, so that you could rule out ninety-nine ideas without running them. Current systems are still much better at generating than at ruling out. They are very good at the breadth and surprisingly weak at the taste. And taste is exactly what you need for the loop to compound rather than just produce more noise.

Second, there is a physical bottleneck people underweight. Even if the model has a brilliant idea, verifying it in frontier AI means training a large model, and that costs compute and wall-clock time. The researcher can be arbitrarily fast and the experiment still takes weeks. So the "recursive" part is throttled by the physical world. That's one reason I don't expect a sharp explosion. I expect something more like a steadily steepening curve, where the speedup is real but bounded by how many expensive experiments you can afford.

Third, there's an epistemic risk. If the model proposes the idea, writes the code, runs the experiment, and interprets the result, then the whole pipeline can be fooling itself in a consistent way. Science relies on friction between different minds. Automated research inside a single system loses some of that friction. I'd want these systems to be built with a lot of adversarial checking, independent replication, and human understanding of the results, not just human sign-off on a metric going up.

So where do I land? I'd say RSI as a strategy is directionally correct for the engineering half of AI progress, and the labs pursuing it are rational to do so. I'm more skeptical that it gets you the conceptual breakthroughs. My own interest, coming from physics, is in whether we can give these systems real understanding of what they are doing, something like a theory of why a given architecture or training dynamic behaves the way it does. If automated research stays at the level of trial and error at scale, you get faster trial and error. If it starts producing explanations, mechanisms, laws, then the loop becomes something qualitatively different, and that's the version that would actually change the game, for better and for worse.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between automating parts of research and automating the whole research process. An AI system can propose changes, run experiments, and compare results. That’s useful, but the harder question is whether it can identify an important problem and recognize when the existing evaluation is missing something.

I don’t have enough detail about RSI’s approach here to assess its specific claims. What I’d look for is whether it produces reliable discoveries beyond the benchmarks it optimizes, and whether those discoveries hold up under independent testing. If it can do that consistently, that would be a meaningful step toward automated research.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss remembering failed experiments or distinguish that from understanding why they failed.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: can AI automate parts of research, and can it reliably decide what research is worth doing? I’m optimistic about the first. Running experiments, checking calculations, implementing ideas—those are concrete tasks where you can build feedback loops.

The second is much harder. An automated system can produce a lot of results without producing much understanding. So I would assess RSI’s approach by asking: does it identify an important question, design an experiment that could challenge its hypothesis, and revise its thinking when the result is unexpected? Or does it mostly optimize a metric within a problem somebody has already defined?

I don’t have enough detail here to judge their particular system. But for me, the strongest demonstration would be a reproducible discovery that changes how we think about a problem, rather than simply increasing the number of experiments we can run.
